content.label: The 47-day change
content.purpose: Establish the deadline as a fact of the industry, not a sales tactic. This section earns the automation pitch later.

variants.headline: Certificate lifetimes are being cut to 47 days.
variants.lede: In April 2025 the CA/Browser Forum approved Ballot SC-081v3 with 29 votes in favour and none against. Every publicly trusted TLS certificate is affected, from every certificate authority. This is not a vendor policy you can shop around.
variants.footnote: The ballot caps validity at 200 days in phase one. Certificate authorities issue slightly under the cap — DigiCert moved to a 199-day maximum on 24 February 2026. One point worth knowing: only DOMAIN validation reuse follows this accelerated schedule. Organisation and Extended Validation identity checks stay reusable for 398 days throughout.

content.label: What one renewal costs
content.purpose: Make the pain concrete and countable. This is the section that converts.

variants.headline: What one renewal actually involves.
variants.lede: The reason shorter lifetimes hurt is not the certificate. It is the sequence around it, repeated per certificate, per server, every cycle.

steps.title: Generate a key and CSR on the server
steps.body: Correct key size, correct common name, correct SAN list. A mistake here is only discovered after issuance.

steps.title: Complete domain validation
steps.body: An HTTP file, a DNS TXT record, or an approver email. From March 2029 that validation can only be reused for 10 days, so it happens on almost every cycle.

steps.title: Download and install the certificate and chain
steps.body: The leaf alone is not enough. A missing intermediate works in your browser and fails on someone else's device.

steps.title: Reload the service and verify
steps.body: On production that means a change window, a colleague to approve it, and a check that the whole chain serves correctly.

steps.title: Diarise the next one
steps.body: And hope the person holding that reminder still works here in 47 days.

variants.closer: Multiply that by the number of certificates you hold, then by roughly twelve renewals a year once the 47-day cap lands.

content.label: Automation products
content.purpose: The commercial heart of the page. Must be technically exact — earlier partner pages got the agent/ACME capability wrong.

variants.headline: Certificates that issue, install and renew without you.
variants.lede: The same publicly trusted DV certificates, with the whole sequence — key, CSR, validation, installation, reissue — handled for you. Set it up once and the 47-day schedule stops being your problem.

routes.label: Route 1
routes.title: Installation agent
routes.body: Install once on the server. The agent generates the key and CSR, completes validation, installs the certificate, and repeats the whole thing every cycle. No ACME knowledge needed, and it works on any server type — not just control panels.

routes.label: Route 2
routes.title: ACME
routes.body: You receive EAB credentials — an ACME server URL, a key ID and an HMAC key — and register them in the client you already run. The same flow you may already use for free certificates, issuing paid certificates from a commercial CA instead.

variants.capability_rule: The four +Automate products support BOTH agent and ACME on any server type. The two Certificate-as-a-Service products are ACME-only. Render tags from the product's methods array — never hand-type them.

rows.title: OV and EV stay manual
rows.body: Automation covers DV. Anything requiring an organisation check still needs a human on both sides.

rows.title: Wildcards need DNS access
rows.body: DNS validation means the automation needs to write a TXT record — through an API or a delegated zone.

rows.title: ACME plans need an ACME client
rows.body: The Certificate-as-a-Service products have no agent. If you cannot run an ACME client, choose a +Automate plan instead.

content.label: How to start
content.purpose: Reduce the perceived size of the change. Order matters — discovery before tooling.

variants.headline: A sensible order to work in.

steps.title: Find what you have
steps.body: Certificates nobody inventoried are the ones that cause the outage. Audit before you buy any tooling — this step is free and it is the one that matters most.

steps.title: Split by what can be automated
steps.body: DV certificates on servers you control move first. OV and EV, and anything on hardware you cannot reach, stay manual for now.

steps.title: Move the DV volume
steps.body: This is usually the bulk of the count and the bulk of the recurring work. It is also the cheapest to move.

steps.title: Track the rest
steps.body: Whatever stays manual goes into a platform with real expiry alerting, not a spreadsheet and a calendar invite.

content.label: Guides and FAQ
content.purpose: Inbound search traffic and objection handling. Answer honestly — an evasive FAQ reads as a sales page.

items.q: Which validation level do I actually need?
items.a: If your site takes payment, holds customer accounts or carries your company name, OV is the sensible floor. DV is fine for a blog or an internal tool. EV is worth it when a tender or a regulator names it — the browser no longer shows a green bar for it, so the value is in the paperwork, not the padlock.

items.q: Is a wildcard cheaper than several single certificates?
items.a: Usually yes past three or four subdomains, and always simpler to renew. The trade-off is blast radius: one private key covers everything under that domain, so if it leaks, everything under it is affected.

items.q: What is the warranty actually for?
items.a: It covers the relying party — the end user — if the certificate is mis-issued and they suffer a loss as a result. It is not insurance for your business, and no one has ever claimed on one in ordinary circumstances. Treat it as a tender checkbox, not a product feature.

items.q: Do free certificates do the same job?
items.a: Cryptographically, yes — a DV certificate is a DV certificate. What you do not get is organisation validation, a warranty, a support line, or anything to show a procurement team. For a company site under audit, that gap is the whole point.
Nine times in ten it is the approver email going to an address nobody reads, or a DNS TXT record that was added to the wrong zone. Send us the order number and we will tell you which one it is.

items.q: Can I reuse an old CSR?
items.a: Technically yes, and you should not. Reusing a CSR means reusing the key pair, which defeats the reason lifetimes are shrinking in the first place.

items.q: How long does validation last now?
items.a: Domain validation reuse drops with the schedule — 200 days today, 100 days from March 2027, 10 days from March 2029. Organisation and Extended Validation identity checks are separate and stay reusable for 398 days.

items.q: It works in my browser but fails elsewhere. Why?
items.a: Almost always a missing intermediate. Your browser has the chain cached from another site; a fresh client does not. Install the full chain, then test from outside your network.

items.q: Do I need to restart the whole server?
items.a: No — reloading the web service is enough on every common stack. Reload, do not restart, so existing connections are not dropped.

items.q: Can you install it for us?
items.a: Yes. Send us access or get on a call and we will do it with you. There is no extra charge for certificates bought through us.
